concepts.name: Gear ratio
concepts.summary: Chainring teeth divided by rear cog teeth: how many times the wheel turns for one pedal turn.

concepts.name: Development
concepts.summary: The distance travelled for one turn of the pedals.

passages.text: Gear ratio is the number of teeth on the chainring divided by the number of teeth on the rear cog. A chainring with 40 teeth driving a cog with 20 teeth gives a gear ratio of 2: the rear wheel turns twice for every full turn of the pedals. A higher ratio is a harder gear.

Cadence is the number of pedal revolutions per minute, written rpm. Most riders settle on a cadence between 70 and 100 rpm on flat ground. Cadence does not say how fast the bicycle goes, because the gear decides how far each pedal turn carries it.

Development is the distance the bicycle travels for one full turn of the pedals. It equals the gear ratio multiplied by the circumference of the wheel. With a gear ratio of 2 and a wheel circumference of 2 metres, the development is 4 metres.

Speed follows from development and cadence: distance per minute equals development multiplied by cadence. Dividing metres per minute by 60 gives metres per second. Changing to a harder gear raises the development, so the same cadence gives a higher speed.
Course logistics: the cycling unit quiz is open for one week after the lecture, and each student may attempt it twice. The better score is kept.

concepts.name: Compound growth
concepts.summary: Interest that is earned on earlier interest as well as on the starting amount.

concepts.name: Growth factor
concepts.summary: One plus the rate: the number the balance is multiplied by each period.

concepts.name: Doubling time
concepts.summary: How long a balance takes to double at a steady rate.

passages.text: Compound growth means that interest is earned on the interest already added as well as on the amount first invested. After each period the balance is multiplied by the same number, so the balance grows faster each period than the one before.

The growth factor is one plus the rate per period, written as a decimal. A rate of 10 percent per period gives a growth factor of 1.10. After n periods the balance is the starting amount times the growth factor raised to the power n.
Doubling time is the number of periods a balance needs to double. A quick estimate is the rule of 72: divide 72 by the rate in percent per period. At 6 percent per period the estimate is 12 periods.
Simple interest differs from compound interest: simple interest is always taken on the starting amount only, so the balance rises by the same amount each period.

concepts.name: Sorted precondition
concepts.summary: Binary search only works when the collection is already in order.

concepts.name: Halving
concepts.summary: Each comparison throws away half of the candidates that remain.

concepts.name: Worst-case comparisons
concepts.summary: The most comparisons the search can need for a given size.

passages.text: Binary search needs the collection to be sorted first. Without the order, comparing with the middle item says nothing about which half can hold the target, so the method gives wrong answers on unsorted data.

Halving is the heart of binary search. Compare the target with the middle item; if they differ, keep only the half in which the target could be and repeat. Each comparison throws away half of the items still in play.
In the worst case binary search needs about log base 2 of n comparisons, rounded up, for n items. Doubling the number of items adds only one more comparison, which is why the method scales so well.
Linear search checks the items one at a time and needs up to n comparisons in the worst case. It works on unsorted data, which binary search cannot handle.
